name: Victor Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Victor. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. This is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the property and trades team at Carver & Mills, a forty-person firm in the city centre. My clients are landlords, plumbers, electricians and a couple of small builders, so it's rental accounts, self-employed tax returns and a lot of van expenses. I use AI tools all day: one reads the receipts, another drafts the tax computations, and I check and sign off.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the tradespeople, because they're straight with you and they work hard. What wears me out is landlords with twelve properties and one shoebox of paperwork. At weekends I do the books for my dad's cash-and-carry, a wholesale warehouse selling to corner shops, and I bought a small rental flat last year with my savings and some family help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a good tool, and the people who use it well get ahead, same as with any tool. At work I'd keep pushing the team to use it. Online I'd post the odd practical tip for small business owners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it suits me fine. I'm well paid, I've got savings and a rental flat, and I'm already faster than most of the team. If AI stays a handy tool, I'll have my own accounting practice by thirty, and my dad will finally stop asking when.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Carver & Mills for two more years while building up private clients from the trades. I'd automate my dad's stock ordering at the cash-and-carry with a simple AI tool. I'd save toward a deposit on a second rental flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and keen to get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would worry you, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interest rates, mainly, because of the rental flat. And my dad's warehouse margins are thin, with the supermarkets undercutting corner shops. Those are business worries, not AI ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you want your own practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because working for yourself is how you build something to pass on. My dad built his warehouse from one van. I'd like to do the same with clients.

The team should **keep using it** for practical work.
think: It **suits me fine**, with savings, a rental flat and faster work.
I'll have my **own practice** by thirty.
do: Build up **private trade clients** while staying two more years.
**Automate stock ordering** at his dad's cash-and-carry.
S0.quote: If AI stays a handy tool, I'll have my own accounting practice by thirty, and my dad will finally stop asking when.
fieldNote: Victor feels **secure**: good pay, savings, a rental flat and strong AI skills.
His existing worries are **interest rates** and his dad's thin warehouse margins.
His drive to **build his own business** comes from his father's example.

steps.text: Take on private plumbers and electricians as evening clients
Set up AI stock ordering at his dad's cash-and-carry
Save toward a deposit on a second rental flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for small firms that move quickly and bad for those that don't. At work I'd say let's be first, not last. I'd tell tradespeople they don't need to pay big fees for simple returns anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I come out ahead. The checking and returns get cheaper, so I can serve twice as many clients on my own. AI makes a one-man accounting practice possible, and that's exactly what I've wanted since I qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave Carver & Mills within a year and start my own practice, with the trades clients I've already built up. I'd run it on AI from day one, keeping fees low. I'd keep the rental flat and put profits into a second one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take clients from Carver & Mills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the ones who come to me. I'd leave on good terms. But if a plumber wants cheaper fees, that's the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older accountants who've never touched these tools, and the juniors who won't get trained. But I'd say the answer is to learn, not to stop it.

fieldNote: Victor sees Steady Disruption as his **opportunity** to go independent.
His **free-market view** shows: cheaper fees are simply the market at work.
He worries for **older colleagues** but believes the answer is learning, not resisting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge shift and people need to move fast, not wait for government. I'd tell my friends to learn a trade or run something real. I'd post that families who work together will be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my accounting work is finished by 2028, practice or no practice. If AI can do almost any thinking work, my clients just use it themselves. My edge was using AI better than other accountants, and AGI makes that edge worth nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move into my dad's cash-and-carry full time and run the business side with AI, while the warehouse still needs people. That's hands-on work, so the robots are about three years behind. I'd hold my savings in cash and keep the rental flat for steady income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have a plan, but the plan has a shelf life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be pleased, honestly. He's wanted me in the business for years. My mum would say I wasted my qualification, but she'd be happy to have me close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in 2031 when the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd own the robots, not be replaced by them, if we play it right. I'd want the warehouse automated by us, so we keep the profit. That's the only way I see a small family business surviving.

Families who **work together** will be fine.

fieldNote: Victor expects his **accounting work** to end fast, despite his AI skills.
His answer is **family business** and ownership, not state help.
The three-year **robot lag** gives the warehouse plan time, but he knows it's limited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to build something, so build it. At work I'd tell people to stop complaining and get ready. I'd still say the market sorts these things out faster than government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a good window. I'd get maybe three years of strong practice earnings and then switch into owning things. Like I said with the fast one, my AI skills aren't permanent, but they're worth a lot right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start my own practice in year one and run it on AI. I'd buy a second rental flat in year two and put money into automating my dad's warehouse. By 2030 I'd sell the practice to a bigger firm if anyone's still buying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly excited. Five years of warning is enough time to build an accounting practice and sell it before AGI makes it worthless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anyone buy an accounting practice in 2030?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not much for it, honestly. But even a small price is better than nothing. And the client list could be useful for selling something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change any family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum keeps asking about marriage. In this version I'd probably settle down around thirty, once the practice is sold and things are clearer.

The **market** sorts this out faster than government.
think: It's a good **window** for three years of practice earnings.
My AI skills **aren't permanent**, but they're valuable now.

S3.quote: Five years of warning is enough time to build an accounting practice and sell it before AGI makes it worthless.
fieldNote: Victor treats five years as a **window to earn**, then **sell**.
He moves wealth into **property** and the family warehouse, which last longer.
His plans for **marriage** wait until the practice is sold.

steps.text: Open an AI-run accounting practice for trades clients

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway and people should use it. At work I'd say learn the tools or start something. I'd tell young people to think like owners, not employees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the best version for me. I'd have eight years of strong earnings, a practice, two or three rental flats and a stake in the family warehouse. I'd be 37 when AGI arrives, owning things instead of selling my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start my practice in year one, grow it and hire one or two juniors who can run AI as well as I do. I'd keep buying rental property and invest in the warehouse's automation. Around year seven I'd start shifting out of accounting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the version where hard work and planning pay off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd hire juniors in a job you expect to vanish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a few years, yes. I'd be honest with them about it, and I'd train them in business, not just accounts. That's worth something whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you marry and start a family in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably around thirty. With ten years and property behind me, I'd feel I could provide properly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it cuts off my practice before I've built it. What would help is lower taxes and less paperwork for small businesses, so people can start things quickly. And easier loans for family businesses buying their own automation.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who owns the machines. The family that owns the warehouse robots will be fine, and the family that works next to the warehouse robots won't be. That's what I'd tell everyone my age.

headlineQuote: The family that owns the warehouse robots will be fine, and the family that works next to the warehouse robots won't be.

Under **AGI by 2028**, he'd join the family warehouse and plan to own its robots.
His **free-market** view runs throughout: think like an owner, not an employee.
